*Knacklaut*de{}wikipedia:langde|Etymology}[knacken]+[Laut]|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈknakˌlaʊ̯t/}Ⓓc/cf/De-Knacklaut.ogg|Noun}(mask.,plural:[Knacklautses])}#phonetics glottal stop}•synononym [[[Glottisschlag],[Glottalplosiv]],[Kehlkopfverschluss]],[Kehlkopfverschlusslaut]}#especially a glottal stop found in null onsets (vowel-initial stems) in German and other languages|Usage notes}It is often claimed that Standard German automatically inserts a glottal stop in null onsets,but this is a myth. Any initial glottal stop may be elided in everyday speech. While such pronunciations may be considered substandard,they by themselves belie the claim of an ''automatic'' glottal stop. More importantly,however,glottal stops in ''unstressed'' onsets are entirely optional and more often than not elided even in formal,careful standard speech.

*knebeln*de{}|Etymology}17th century,derived from Knebel,from Middle High German knebel,from Old High German knebil. The word originally meant a stick used to tighten a tie or to bind something to,later also the tie itself. from Dutch knevelen shows the same semantic development,being used chiefly for “to gag”,but also in the broader sense “to tie up”.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈkneːbəln/}Ⓓf/f3/De-knebeln.ogg|Verb}de-verb}#transitive to gag gloss:tie a piece of cloth around someone’s mouth to prevent them from shouting}#transitive to hog-tie gloss:tie up someone’s arms and legs to prevent them from moving}#}knebeln An Händen und Füßen '''geknebelt''',der Mund verklebt,verscharrt in einem Papp-Sarg – ein Horror!}•'''Hog-tied''' at your hands and feet,adhesive tape over your mouth,buried in a cardboard coffin—a horror!}#transitive to hog-tie; to render helpless; to oppress; to enslave|Usage notes}Most dictionaries give only the sense “to gag”,but the sense “to hog-tie” is attestable from Early Modern German to the present. Often both ideas also go hand in hand,especially in the combination gefesselt und geknebelt. Note that fesseln as such is broader in meaning,as it can also mean “to handcuff” or “to tie to something immovable”,which  never does.|Derived terms}Knebelvertrag

*Kneipchen*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈknaɪ̯pçən/|Etymology 1}Kneipe|Noun}(neut.)}#Kneipe:small pub,bar|Noun}(neut.)}#Hessian small knife
*Kneipe*de{}|Etymology}From kneipen,an archaic variant of kneifen.}The noun spread from student slang of Upper Saxony in the later 18th century,possibly picked up from thieves’ cant,and is based on the idea of a crowded pub where people,as it were,squeeze and poke each other. ''Kneipe'' became the commonest word for “pub” during the 20th century.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈknaɪ̯pə/}Ⓓd/db/De-Kneipe.ogg|Noun}(fem.)}#pub,bar}•synononym Thesaurus:Kneipe}#obsolete a student’s cramped dwelling|Usage notes}The term ''Kneipe'' typically refers to a pub that does not serve hot food,which is the predominant rule for pubs in German-speaking Europe. Pubs that do serve hot food are more likely to be referred to as Wirtschaft or Lokal,although they may also be called ''Kneipe''.|Derived terms}kneipenartig|Descendants}desctree:bor1}desctree:bor1

*Knifte*de{}|Etymology}From Knift,a word found in several Central German dialects,sometimes meaning "large knife",sometimes "slice of bread". The word meaning "knife" is probably derived from Middle Low German knîf,also from Middle High German knîf (West Central German),both from Proto-Germanic ⋆knībaz (whence also from English knife). The sense "rifle" can be explained from this via "weapon" or "bayonet". The word meaning "slice of bread" may be identical (via "cut off"),or otherwise a related form.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈknɪftə/}Ⓓa/a2/De-Knifte.ogg|Noun}(fem.)}#military rifle}#colloquial thick slice of bread

*knirschen*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German gnashing. Cognate with from Dutch to gnash,crash.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈknɪʁʃn̩/}Ⓓ3/3c/De-knirschen.ogg|Verb}de-verb}#sound to scrunch,to crunch}#one's teeth to gnash,to grind}#figurative to be wrathful,(English),to pent-up,(English) anger}•synononym [grollen],[grimmen]}#}knirschen Der Untergang der Griechischen Staaten hat aber noch das Eigenthümliche,dass er mehr einem gewaltsamen,als einem Krankheitstode gleicht,wo das Leben erst weicht,nachdem die Kraft schon erloschen ist. Die wahre Periode des Verfalls Griechenlands war schon die Regierung Philipps und Alexanders; nicht bloss die innere Freiheit,sondern auch die äussere Unabhängigkeit war damals schon zum Namen geworden; und doch lebten in dieser Periode Praxiteles und Apelles; die feinste Blüthe Atheniensischer Beredsamkeit entwickelte sich in Isocrates,Aeschines und Demosthenes; Aristoteles erstieg den Gipfel seiner Grösse,und Plato reicht bis an diese Zeit. Auch an weiser und unternehmender Staatsklugheit,an reiner Vaterlandsliebe,an ausharrendem Muthe,an ewig gegen seine Fesseln '''knirschendem''' Freiheitssinn fehlte es weder damals,noch lange nachher,wie die Schlachten von w:Battle of Chaeronea (338 BC):Chäronea und w:Battle of Crannon:Cranon,die Unbiegsamkeit der Thebaner gegen Alexander,später Philopömenes und Aratus,und die verzweifelte Gegenwehr Athens gegen Sylla bezeugen.

*Knofi*de{}|Etymology}A diminutive form pertaining to Knoblauch. The ''-f-'' is due to its being derived from dialectal forms. One would expect a from German Low German - origin (cf. from Middle Low German knoflōk),but there are also forms with ''-f-'' in some southern German dialects (themselves from Old High German chlovalouh). Southern origin is more likely given the regional form Knofel,but Low German would have helped to spread the form in the north.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈknoːfi/}IPA:aaless common|Noun}(mask.)}#colloquial garlic}•synononym [[[Knoblauch<g:m)],[;]],[Knofel (southern Germany]],[ Austria)<g:m)]

*Knoten*de{}slim-wikipedia:langde|Etymology}From Middle High German knote,from Middle High German knode,from Old High German knoto,from Old High German knodo.}The two forms are probably variants based on Grammatischer Wechsel. The form with ''-t-'' (from Proto-Germanic ''}-d-'') was predominant in East Central German,that with ''-d-'' (from Proto-Germanic ''}-þ-'') in Upper German. Incidentally,this situation explains the lengthened vowel in the standardized form (lengthening being blocked before ''-t-'' in Upper German,but not in Central German). Neither German form can be derived directly from Proto-Germanic ⋆knuttô,whence from Middle High German knotze and from English knot,though a relation is very likely.}The senses “journeyman”,“person (of some quality)” are probably due,at least in part,to conflation with from Middle Low German mate,companion,cognate of Cognate German Genosse. Alongside,there is a common tendency of referring to people,especially children,with words for thick,plump,or inflated objects (compare e.g. Balg).|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈknoːtn̩}Ⓓ9/98/De-Knoten.ogg|Noun}(mask.,diminituve:[KnotenKnötchen])}#knot gloss:looping}#knot gloss:swelling}#Austria interchange gloss:motorway junction}#nautical knot gloss:unit of speed}#graph theory vertex,node}#obsolete craftsman; journeyman; farmhand}#in compounds a person of some specified quality or practice; chiefly in l+de+Furzknoten,but sometimes other colloquial formations|Synonyms}sense:interchange Dreieck; Autobahndreieck; Kreuz; Autobahnkreuz}sense:in graph theory Ecke|Hyponyms}Autobahnknoten}Fruchtknoten}Gordischer Knoten}Haarknoten}Nervenknoten}Schuhbandknoten|Derived terms}knotig

*kochen*de{}|Etymology}from Proto-Indo-European ⋆pekʷ-}From Middle High German kochen,from Old High German kohhōn,from Proto-West Germanic tto cook.}posin general did this term get the much more limited and specific sense of "to boil"?|Pronunciation}IPA:-xŋ̍}Ⓓb/b5/De-kochen.ogg}Ⓓb/b5/De-kochen2.ogg}De-at-kochen.ogg(Austria)|Verb}de-verb}#intransitive to cook,to prepare food (chiefly hot food for lunch or supper)}#transitive to cook something (in a) liquid (e.g. soup,chili,spaghetti)}#to boil}#intransitive gloss:to reach the boiling point}#transitive gloss:to heat a liquid until it boils}#intransitive to be stirred up or agitated,especially with anger|Usage notes}Intransitive  can be used for all sorts of food preparation that require at least some amount of work and effort. However,there is a strong tendency to use the verb only for the preparation of a proper dinner,be it lunch or supper. Hence,the preparation of,say,an onion tart for dinner is ,even though the food is baked. Contrarily,the preparation of breakfast is only rarely called  even if eggs are boiled in the process.}Transitive  can generally be used only for actual boiling. Hence,would be understood solely as dropping a steak into a pot of boiling water.|Synonyms}sense:of a liquid:to boil sieden}sense:make a liquid boil sieden}sense:prepare food in boiling liquid garen broader|Derived terms}Kochfeld}abkochen}auch nur mit Wasser kochen}aufkochen}einkochen}überkochen}verkochen}vorkochen}nachkochen}hart kochen}weich kochen|See also}erwärmen}erhitzen}dampfen}qualmen}rauchen}brodeln

*kommste heut nicht, kommste morgen*de{}|Alternative forms}less common; rendered in formal Standard German|Etymology}lit:if you don't come today,you'll come tomorrow.}Some sources trace it back to Colognian m:küss de hück nit,küss de morje,but the saying is attested in various dialect dictionaries. (Colognians are by stereotype easygoing and workshy,which may be the reason for the association.) Compare also cog:kom ik er vandaag niet,dan kom ik er morgen.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˌkɔmstə ˈhɔʏ̯t nɪç(t) ˌkɔmstə ˈmɔʁɡən/|Phrase}kommste heut nicht,kommste morgen:}#ng:expresses a hands-off,easygoing attitude,especially with respect to time; depending on the context it may be positive/neutral or negative (then implying tardiness or unreliability)}•Du hast noch 60 Euro auf deinem Deckel! Aber kein Stress:'''Kommste heut nicht,kommste morgen.'''}•You still have 60 euro on your slate! But no worries:You can pay it whenever you have it on you.}•Die Busse fahren hier nach der Devise:'''Kommste heut nicht,kommste morgen.'''}•

Denn auf dem Kopfe tragen sie eine hohe Mütze von Birkenrinde in Gestalt eines abgestumpften Kegels,welche mit blauem Tuche überzogen und auf der vordern Seite dicht mit Silbermünzen besetzt ist. Über die selbe wird ein großes weißes,an den Ecken mit Figuren ausgenähtes und mit rothen Frangen eingefaßtes Tuch gehängt,so daß der kurze Zipfel vorn über die Mütze,der lange aber über den Rücken hinabhängt,während die Seitentheile auf den Schultern ruhen. For on the head they wear a high cap of birch bark in the shape of a truncated cone,which is overlaid by blue cloth and on the front side stuffed with silver coins. Over the self-same they hang a large white blanket sewn out on the corners with figures and framed with fringes,so that the short cusp hangs ahead down the cap,but the long one down the back,while the side parts rest on the shoulders. Under this '''head finery''' the hair is rolled together and hidden,for they shun letting it see and lay themselves,when foreigners spend the night in the house,with this '''head finery''' to bed,as they also do their work in the animal stable with it; this '''head finery''' is called <span style"letter-spacing:0.1em">Aischon</span> with them.}#}Kopfputz Am 5. *Korb*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German korp,from Old High German korb,from Old High German chorp,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆korb.}The sense “rejection of a (romantic) request” is formed back from the expressions einen Korb geben,einen Korb kriegen. These derive from certain older customs,which involved a bottomless basket as a symbol of the end or inexistence of love. The further origin of this symbol seems uncertain,though it has been plausibly related to the apparent mediaeval practice of pulling a secret visitor up to one’s window in a basket. *Kran*de{}wikipedia:langde|Etymology}From Middle High German krane,from Old High German tcrane,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆kranō,from Proto-Germanic tcrane.}The word was used metaphorically for the lifting device due to the similar appearance of the bird’s neck and head. This metaphorical use is first attested in from Middle Dutch krane,and thence spread to several European languages (compare from English crane,from French grue). The sense “water tap” is restricted to a smaller territory (compare from Dutch kraan,from Luxembourgish Krunn).|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈkʁaːn/}Ⓓc/c6/De-Kran.ogg}Rhymes:aːn|Noun}(mask.,genitive:Kranes,plural:[Kränee])}#crane gloss:a lifting device}•Bei Sturm darf ein '''Kran''' nicht umfallen.}•A '''crane''' must not fall over in the event of a storm.}#regional tap,faucet}•synononym [[Hahn],[Wasserhahn]],[Pipe]}•Der '''Kran''' in der Küche tropft.}•The '''tap''' in the kitchen is dripping.|Derived terms}Kraneberger|Descendants}}:}:

*kreischen*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German krīschen,from Old High German ⋆krīskan,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆krīskan,from Proto-Germanic tto cry out,shout,from Proto-Indo-European tto shout. According to Pfeifer,this is an extension of from Proto-Indo-European tto cry hoarsely,which makes it cognate with dated/obsolete Cognate German tto cry in pain,give birth. *Kretscham*de{}2018|Etymology}From Middle High German kretscheme,from a from German - language,from Proto-Slavic ⋆kъrčьma. Doublet of Kaschemme.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈkrɛt͡ʃam/}Ⓓ7/78/De-Kretscham.ogg|Noun}(mask.)}#Silesia a village inn or tavern}#}Kretscham Ich schloy mich och biß weeln im ganzen '''Kratschem'''  mit Knaichten unde Bouren rümm unde mache doß der Balbir unde der Bader ze thun/unde de Gerichte ze besichtigen bekummen.:seriesKomedia. Deutsche Lustspiele vom Barock bis zur Gegenwart 4:translationSometimes I brawl about in the whole '''inn''' with haulers and peasants and make that the barber and the barber-surgeon get ado and the courts get to assess.}#}Kretscham Am Trauungstage war Sammlung,d. h. die Gäste des Bräutigams versammelten sich Nachmittags im Gerichts'''kretscham''',nahmen einen Trunk Bier,ließen solchen auch den anderen Anwesenden,Nichthochzeitsgästen,reichen. Auch dem dabei nicht anwesenden Pfarrer wurden einige Kannen Bier gut geschrieben. Aus dem '''Kretscham''' ging man nun ins Brauthaus,wo der Hochzeitbitter als Redner auftrat; von da zog man feierlich,oft unter Glockengeläute,oft mit vorangehender Musik in die Kirche. Braut und Bräutigam wurden jedes von 2 sogenannten Brautführern an das Altar geleitet und nach der Trauung zurückgeführt; auch hatten beide Brautleute Züchtjungfern,kleine,auch mit Kränzen geschmückte Mädchen. Wie in die Kirche,zog aus derselben man zurück ins Hochzeitshaus,meist das Haus der Braut. Dort waren die Tische schon gedeckt,man setzte sich bald,nicht in bunter Reihe,sondern nach Geschlechtern und genoß eine Menge von Gerichten. War der Pfarrer anwesend,so sprach er das Tischgebet,sonst der Hochzeitbitter und stundenlangen Sitzen wurde das Essen mit dem Gesange eines Liederverses,gewöhnlich:Lob und Ehr und Preis ꝛc. und vorher gesprochenem Gebete,beschlossen. Dann hielt der Hochzeitbitter im Namen der Brautleute eine Dankrede,an deren Schlusse er zum Beschenken des Brautpaares aufforderte,auch zum sogenannten Bierzuge,d. h. er lud ein in den '''Kretscham''' zu ziehen,was Herrschaft und '''Kretscham'''besitzer fordern konnten,doch mit dem Zusatze:„Wem es sein Amt,oder Stand,oder sonst etwas nicht gestattet,wolle sichs noch länger bei Speise und Trank im Hochzeithause gefallen lassen. Im '''Kretscham''' waren noch viele Personen anwesend,freien Trunk erwartend,und nicht blos die Brautleute,sondern auch die Hochzeitsgäste ließen fleißig einschenken. Hatte man bei der Hochzeit Musik,so wurde im '''Kretscham''' auch getanzt.|Derived terms}Kretschmar,Kretschmer

*Krug*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:/kruːk/}IPA:aanorthern and central Germany,now chiefly colloquial}Rhymes:uːkuːx|Etymology 1}From Middle High German kruoc,from Old High German kruog,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆krōgu,from Proto-Germanic ⋆krōguz. Immediate cognates are from Middle Dutch croech,from Old English crōg,of obscure origin. Possibly from a from Proto-Indo-European - root shared with from Old Armenian pitcher,large jar,from Ancient Greek pitcher,but the phonetics are problematic.  Also compare from Old Irish skin.}The originally Low German Kruke,cognate with from English crock,is another word,though a relation with ''Krug'' is considered likely.|Noun}(mask.,genitive:Kruges,plural:[Krüge],diminituve:Krug)}#jug}•synononym Kanne|Etymology 2}From Middle Low German krôch,from Middle Low German krûch,whence from German Low German Kroog and through borrowing from Dutch pub,from Swedish krog. Further origin unknown. A relation with etymology 1 cannot be ruled out,but is considered unlikely by most authorities.|Noun}(mask.,genitive:Kruges,plural:[Krüge])}#dated pub; bar}•synononym Kneipe (see there for further synonyms)|Usage notes}The simplex has now become rare. The compound Dorfkrug remains in use for the central pub or inn of a village. The word is also still found in the names of many traditional pubs in northern Germany.|Derived terms}Nobiskrug

*Kugel*de{}'''Kugeln'''|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈkuːɡəl/|Etymology 1}}From Middle High German kugel,from Middle High German kugele,of from German nocap1 origin,but probably related to Keule.}de Possibly from Proto-Germanic tknobbed instrument,a derivative offrom Proto-Germanic tcog,swelling,from Proto-Indo-European tswelling,bow,an extension of from Proto-Indo-European tto bow,bend,arch,curve”,whence also perhaps from Albanian tacorn,small ball.}Further discussion}Outside of loans from German (as in from Danish kugle and from Dutch kogel),it appears only in German,and only from the Middle High German period,as ''kugel,kugele'',referring to a ball used in games (Spielkugel).}Nevertheless,the word seems to be of genuinely from German - origin. A Swiss dialect form has an additional ''r'',in ''krugle'',found already in Middle High German in the diminutive form ''krúgellin'' (Konrad of Würzburg,d. 1287).}Middle German variants of the word in the original sense “ball used in skittles or Paille-maille” are ''kaule,kulle'',while Low German had cognates of Klotz.}The sense “bullet” is directly via comparison with the ball in skittles,already in use for lead or iron spheres used as projectiles (fired with slingshots or similar) before firearms became widespread.}Also compared are Kegel,as well as from English cudgel and from English cog,though these connections are far from certain.}{{rel-bottom|Noun}(fem.,diminituve:Kugel)}#ball defdate:13th century}#firearms bullet,projectile defdate:15th century}•synononym [Projektil],[Geschoss]}•Die '''Kugel''' ging mitten ins Herz.}•The '''bullet''' went right through the heart.}#firearms round,cartridge,bullet}•synononym Patrone}•Er hatte noch drei '''Kugeln''' im Magazin.}•He had three '''rounds''' left in the magazine.}#astronomy orb,globe,celestial body defdate:16th century}#geometry sphere,orb defdate:16th century}•synononym Sphäre}#heraldiccharge roundel of any tincture}#of icecream scoop|Usage notes}The German words ''Kugel'' and Ball are distinguished inasmuch as the former refers to solid balls (such as those used for billiards or bowling) while the latter refers to air-filled or elastic balls (such as tennis or soccer balls). This distinction may be neglected colloquially or jokingly.|Derived terms}kugeln}kugelig}kuglicht}verkugeln|Hyponyms}Babykugel}Bowlingkugel}Erdkugel}Glaskugel}Gewehrkugel}Halbkugel}Kristallkugel}Mottenkugel}Schrotkugel}Christbaumkugel}Weihnachtskugel}Weihnachtsbaumkugel}Weltkugel}Zielkugel|Noun}(fem.)}#nocap1

*Kupfernickel*de{}|Etymology}From [[[Kupfer]+[t1copper]]+[Nickel]]+[t2mischievious spirit or demon]. This word originated as a pejorative German term for ores of the element nickel,whose bright green color closely resembles malachite,an otherwise reliable indicator of valuable copper ore. However,like iron,nickel ore is impossible to smelt at the relatively low temperatures needed to smelt copper. (This is also why the Copper Age preceded the Iron Age.) Annoyed at wasting their time on such ore,German miners began calling it <i>cupfernickel</i>,that is,"copper demon." When chemists eventually identified and named the element in the ore,they shortened the name of the ore to <i>nickel</i>. The name of this element thus has the same roots as the phrase "Old Nick," which refers to a supreme devil or demon. Feeling a bit whimsical,chemists of that same period named another newly isolated iron-like element,cobalt,after a mischievous German household spirit,the "kobold."|Noun}(neut.)}#cupronickel

("in the context of ''Waltharius'',c. AD 920 the long-sword spatha was worn on a baldric on the left hip,the half-sword scramasax on the right,usually attached to the mail-shirt hauberk with chains.") *lassen*de{}|Alternative forms}obsolete|Etymology}From Middle High German lāzen,from Old High German lāzan,from Proto-West Germanic tto let,allow,from Proto-Germanic to leave behind,allow,from Proto-Indo-European to let,leave behind. Cognates include from Bavarian låssn,from Dutch laten,from English let.|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈlasən}De-lassen.ogg(Germany)}De-at-lassen.ogg(Austria)}las+sen|Verb}lassen(lässt#ließ,gelassen:lassenwith an infinitive)}#transitive to allow; to permit; to let}•lasset alle Hoffnung fahren}•abandon all hope}#auxiliary to have someone (do something); to have (something done); to make (something happen); to cause (something to be done)}•Wir haben neue Schränke für die Küche machen '''lassen'''.}•We '''had''' new cabinets made for the kitchen.}•Hast du dir die Haare schneiden '''lassen'''?}•Did you '''get''' your hair cut?}•Ich '''ließ''' den Nachbarn die Blumen gießen. (active) - Ich '''ließ''' die Blumen (vom Nachbarn) gießen. (passive)}•I '''made''' the neighbor water the flowers. - I '''had''' the flowers watered (by the neighbor).}#transitive to let remain,to leave (in a certain state)}•Mir ist es lieber,meine Haare grau zu '''lassen'''.}•I prefer to '''leave''' my hair grey.}#transitive to stop (something); to quit; to refrain from; to help doing (something)}#intransitive to cease; to desist|Usage notes}Note that the English phrases "to ''let'' someone do something" and "to ''make'' someone do something" both translate into German as ''jemanden etwas tun lassen''. In order to avoid ambiguity,"to let" can be expressed as ''jemandem erlauben,etwas zu tun'' or ''zulassen,dass jemand etwas tut'',while "to make" can be expressed as ''jemanden dazu bringen,etwas zu tun'' or ''dafür sorgen,dass jemand etwas tut''.}In perfect tenses,''lassen''+infinitive takes a double-infinitive construction,i.e. both verbs are in the infinitive:''Ich habe mir die Haare schneiden lassen.'' (“I’ve had my hair cut.”). Beck:locationMünchen}#intransitive to pass; to flow|Usage notes}Some dictionaries misleadingly define ''laufen'' as specifically meaning a pace between gehen and rennen. This was the original sense in Middle High German,and this is still common in Bavaria and Austria. But descriptions or definitions that claim it has only this meaning are contradicted by long-established usage. In fact,''laufen'' is neutral with regard to pace in modern German,unless the context implies it,as in:}Regardless of pace,moreover,only  is commonly used of animals and in such idioms as  or m:tto learn to walk.}In Austria,however,''laufen'' is not considered neutral with regard to pace,and a strict distinction is made between gehen,which is exclusively used in the sense of “to walk”,and ''laufen'' and rennen,both of which are exclusively used in the sense of “to run”.|Derived terms}ablaufen}Amok laufen}anlaufen}auf dem Laufenden}auf Hochtouren laufen}auflaufen}aus dem Ruder laufen}auslaufen}belaufen}davonlaufen}durchlaufen}einlaufen}eislaufen or Eis laufen}entlanglaufen}entlaufen}erlaufen}Gefahr laufen}herablaufen}herauflaufen}herauslaufen}hereinlaufen}herlaufen}herüberlaufen}herumlaufen}herunterlaufen}hinablaufen}hinauflaufen}hinauslaufen}hineinlaufen}hinlaufen}hinüberlaufen}hinunterlaufen}ins Leere laufen}ins Messer laufen}ins offene Messer laufen}Lauf}Läufer}läufig}leerlaufen}loslaufen}mitlaufen}nachlaufen}rauflaufen}rauslaufen}reinlaufen}rüberlaufen}rumlaufen}überlaufen}umlaufen}unterlaufen}verlaufen}volllaufen}vorlaufen}weglaufen}wundlaufen}zerlaufen}zulaufen}zurücklaufen|See also}gehen}rennen

*lebendig*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German lëbendic,from Old High German lëbēntīg. Equivalent to lebend+ig.}The word originally had normal stress on the initial syllable,as is still the case in from Dutch levendig,from Yiddish לעבעדיק,and in some dialectal German forms such as from Hunsrik levendich. The shift to the second syllable is first attested in the 16th century; it had established itself as the sole standard by the mid-18th century.<ref name"Weigand">Weigand,''Deutsches Wörterbuch'' (1860)</ref> While such shifts happened more often in modern German (compare Forelle,Holunder,Wacholder),the case of  is peculiar in that it is a transparent formation rather than a word whose derivation had become obscure.|Pronunciation}IPA:lə- qualifier:standard}Ⓓ7/7a/De-lebendig2.ogg}IPA:/leˈbɛndɪk/qualifier:common form in southern Germany,Austria,and Switzerland}Ⓓ2/2d/De-lebendig.ogg}Ⓓ1/12/De-lebendig3.ogg|Adjective}#living,alive,animate}•synononym [lebend],[am Leben]}#lively,vivacious,spirited,animated,vibrant,active,agile}•synononym lebhaft|Derived terms}quicklebendig}springlebendig

*leiden*de{}|Alternative forms}laiden|Etymology}From Middle High German līden,from Old High German līdan,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆līþan,from Proto-Germanic ⋆līþaną. Cognate with from Dutch lijden,from English lithe. The sense developed from “go,travel” via “endure” to “suffer”. This happened under the influence of from Middle High German tto be sorry,suffer,be hated,from Old High German leidēn,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆laiþijan,and also the originally unrelated noun Leid,which is cognate with from English loath.|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈlaɪ̯dn̩}Ⓓ2/2f/De-leiden.ogg}Ⓓ2/23/De-leiden2.ogg|Verb}leiden(litt,gelitten)}#intransitive to suffer,to experience pain,sorrow,etc.}•Lerne '''leiden''' ohne zu klagen.}•Learn '''to suffer''' without complaining.}#transitive to suffer,bear,endure,undergo,experience (some hardship)}•Er '''litt''' höllische Qualen.}•He '''suffered''' hellish torment.}#intransitive to suffer leiden ( with  :an(dat)from a disease or condition)}•Die Gefangenen '''leiden''' an Unterernährung.}•The prisoners '''suffer''' from malnutrition.}#}quote-journal:archivedate12 April 2013}#transitive to like,tolerate}•Ich kann ihn einfach nicht '''leiden'''!}•I just can't '''stand''' him!|Derived terms}durchleiden}erleiden}Leiden}Leidenschaft}mitleiden}verleiden
